hints: All three are halogens in one group
Count the electron shells in each atom
More shells means a larger atom

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionisation energy rises across but falls down
paragraphs: Ionisation energy is the toll paid to remove an electron. Across a period, each new proton is added to the same electron shell, so every electron feels a stronger pull. The toll therefore rises steadily from sodium to chlorine.

Down a group, each new element adds a whole shell outside the previous one. The outer electrons are not only farther away but shielded by inner shells, so the pull weakens and the toll falls. Potassium costs less to ionise than lithium for exactly this reason.
The trend pauses at the noble gases, whose full shells make a sudden jump in cost. That saw-tooth shape confirms the rule: shell structure, not mass alone, sets the price of removing an electron.
A candidate who explains the trend with charge-versus-shielding language earns full marks; a candidate who recites 'it increases' without the reason earns only part. The mechanism is the mark.
A candidate who explains the trend with charge-versus-shielding language earns full marks; a candidate who recites ‘it increases’ without the reason earns only part. The mechanism is the mark.
The same contest also sets electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character, so one explanation carries several items.
bullets: Across a period, charge wins and ionisation energy rises.
Down a group, shielding wins and ionisation energy falls.
Noble gases mark the peaks of the saw-tooth trend.
Reasons earn marks; recitation earns part marks.

content.heading: Go deeper: Why atomic radius falls across but rises down
paragraphs: Atomic radius is the distance from nucleus to outer electron. Across a period, protons increase while the shell stays the same, so the pull per electron grows and the atom shrinks. Sodium is larger than chlorine for this reason alone.

Down a group, a new shell is added each step, so even though protons increase, the outer electrons sit a whole layer farther out. Fluorine is therefore much smaller than bromine, despite having fewer protons.
Ionic radius follows the same contest with a twist: Na⁺ is smaller than the Na atom because it lost a shell, while Cl⁻ is larger than Cl because it gained one. Charge changes the shell count itself.
That twist is why radius questions often ask about ions rather than atoms. A candidate who converts the charge into a shell change before comparing will never be trapped.
Radius values quoted for ions come from crystal measurements, and they follow the shell logic exactly: fewer shells, smaller ion; more shells, larger ion.
bullets: Across a period, atoms shrink as protons are added.
Down a group, atoms grow as shells are added.
Na⁺ shrank a shell; Cl⁻ gained one.
Convert the charge to a shell change first.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in the periodic table
paragraphs: The classic trap reverses the two directions: candidates recall that electronegativity rises across the period and then apply that rise down the group, where it actually falls. Before answering, the candidate must name the direction — across or down — and only then choose the rising or falling trend.

The second trap is metallic character. It fades across the period (left is metallic, right is non-metallic) and grows down the group (heavier members are more metallic). Both statements are true; confusing which direction the question asks about is the error.

The third trap is position versus properties. A candidate may state that Group 1 elements 'are reactive' without explaining that each has one outer electron to lose. The charge-versus-shielding mechanism is what earns the full mark.
The fourth trap is reading 'increase' as 'decrease' on a downward question. Writing the two arrows — across ↑, down ↓ — beside every trend question removes this error almost entirely.
bullets: Name the direction before choosing the trend.
Metallic character fades across, grows down.
Reasons (charge vs shielding) earn the full mark.
Write the arrows beside every trend item.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding
lessons.objective: Distinguish electrovalent (ionic), covalent, coordinate, hydrogen, metallic bonds and van der Waals forces, deduce bond types from electron configurations, relate bonding to properties of compounds, and differentiate the shapes of simple molecules (linear, non-linear, tetrahedral, pyramidal).

content.heading: Chemical Bonding
paragraphs: A mango seller ties a bunch with a short string: sharing. Another counts out coins and hands them over: giving. Atoms do the same two things with electrons — sharing them or giving them — and everything about compounds comes from choosing between those two acts.

content.heading: Giving and sharing electrons
paragraphs: Electrovalent (ionic) bonding is giving: a metal loses electrons and a non-metal gains them, so both become ions that attract each other. Sodium (2,8,1) gives one electron and chlorine (2,8,7) gains one, forming NaCl. The result is a lattice, like a criss-cross of opposite charges.

Covalent bonding is sharing: non-metals share electrons so each reaches a full outer shell. Two hydrogen atoms share their electrons to form H₂, and oxygen shares two pairs to form O₂. Water (H₂O) and methane (CH₄) are covalent because all their atoms are non-metals.

Ionic compounds melt high and conduct when molten or dissolved, because their ions are free to move. Covalent compounds usually melt low and never conduct, because they have no ions to move. Properties therefore announce the bonding.
bullets: Ionic = giving electrons (metal + non-metal).
Covalent = sharing electrons (non-metal + non-metal).
Ionic: high melting, conducts molten. Covalent: low melting, no conduction.
Properties announce the bonding.
content.takeaway: Giving makes ions and crystals; sharing makes molecules; properties tell which.

check.question: Magnesium (2,8,2) and chlorine (2,8,7) react. Which bonding results, and how many of each ion form?
options: Ionic bonding, one Mg²⁺ and two Cl⁻
Ionic bonding, one Mg⁺ and one Cl⁻
check.why: Magnesium loses two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and two chlorines each gain one to become Cl⁻.

content.heading: The special bonds
paragraphs: Metallic bonding is giving without keeping: metal atoms drop their outer electrons into a shared sea, and the sea holds the positive cores together. That shared sea is why metals conduct electricity and bend instead of breaking.

Hydrogen bonding is an extra attraction between molecules, not a bond inside one. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other, which is why water boils so high compared with similar small molecules. A coordinate (dative) bond is sharing where both electrons come from one atom, as in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ and [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺.

Van der Waals forces are the weakest attractions between molecules, like the faint stickiness of loose pages. They matter only when stronger bonds are absent, which is why they are mentioned as a special weak force.
bullets: Metallic = shared electron sea; explains conductivity and malleability.
Hydrogen bond = extra attraction between molecules (water, HF, NH₃).
Coordinate bond = sharing where one atom supplies both electrons.
Van der Waals = weakest force between molecules.
content.takeaway: Metallic seas, hydrogen attractions and dative sharing are the special cases.

check.question: In [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, where do the bonding electron pairs come from?
options: One comes from Cu and one from NH₃
Both come from the NH₃ molecules
Both come from the copper ion
They are free electrons shared by the sea
check.why: In a coordinate bond one atom supplies both electrons — here NH₃ supplies each pair.

content.heading: Shapes of molecules
paragraphs: The shape of a molecule depends on how its atoms arrange around the centre. A linear molecule is a straight line, like CO₂, HCl, H₂, O₂ and Cl₂. A bent (non-linear) molecule folds at the centre, like H₂O, which is why its shape is V-shaped.

A tetrahedral molecule spreads four atoms to the corners of a pyramid, like CH₄. A trigonal pyramidal molecule spreads three atoms with a lone pair at the apex, like NH₃. The lone pair pushes the three atoms down, giving the pyramid its shape.

Shape predicts properties: bent water is polar while linear CO₂ is not, and tetrahedral methane is symmetrical and non-polar. A candidate who can picture the shape can predict polarity without memorising it.
bullets: Linear: CO₂, HCl, H₂, O₂, Cl₂ (straight line).
Bent: H₂O (folds at oxygen).
Tetrahedral: CH₄ (four corners). Pyramidal: NH₃ (apex up).
Shape predicts polarity.
content.takeaway: Counting the arrangement around the centre names the shape.

check.question: Which molecule has a tetrahedral shape?
check.why: Methane spreads its four hydrogen atoms to the corners of a tetrahedron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Decide bonding from the electron counts first: a metal losing electrons means ionic, two non-metals sharing means covalent. The count decides before the name does.

content.problem: Deduce the bonding in MgCl₂ from the electron counts Mg (2,8,2) and Cl (2,8,7).

steps.reason: Magnesium has 2 outer electrons; chlorine needs 1 to fill its shell
A metal always gives; its 2 electrons go to two chlorines
One Mg²⁺ balances two Cl⁻, and ionic solids melt high

content.question: Sodium (2,8,1) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7). Deduce the bonding, the ions formed and the formula.
hints: Sodium is a metal — what does it do with its one electron?
Chlorine needs one electron — so one sodium feeds one chlorine
Write the ions, then drop the charges into the formula

content.heading: Go deeper: Why ionic compounds conduct only when molten or dissolved
paragraphs: In solid NaCl, the ions are locked in a rigid lattice and cannot move, so no current flows even though charges are present. Melting or dissolving frees the ions to drift to the electrodes, and conduction begins. Conductivity is therefore about freedom of ions, not the mere presence of charge.

Covalent compounds never conduct, even molten, because they contain no ions at all — only neutral molecules. Diamond and graphite differ here because graphite has free electrons between its layers, a rare covalent exception.

A candidate can be tested on the prediction, not the definition: given a new compound's melting point and conductivity, name its bonding. High melting plus conduction when molten means ionic; low melting with no conduction means covalent.
That prediction skill is exactly what JAMB questions measure. Bonding names, shapes and properties are one chain, and the chain starts at the electron count.
The same logic runs backwards: when a solution is evaporated, the ions lock back into a lattice and conduction stops. Freedom of ions is switched on and off by state, not by composition.
JAMB items exploit this directly, asking why solid NaCl fails to conduct while its melt succeeds. The answer is always the locked ions, never the absence of charge.
bullets: Solid ionic: ions locked, no conduction.
Molten or dissolved: ions free, conduction starts.
Covalent: no ions at all, so no conduction ever.
Predict bonding from melting point and conductivity.

content.heading: Go deeper: Hydrogen bonding versus ordinary dipole forces
paragraphs: Ordinary dipole attraction happens between any polar molecules: the positive end of one is faintly attracted to the negative end of another. Hydrogen bonding is a stronger, special case that needs a hydrogen atom bonded directly to N, O or F.

That is why water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C while methane (CH₄), of similar size, boils far lower. Each water molecule hydrogen-bonds to its neighbours, and much heat is needed to break those links. HF and NH₃ show the same elevation.

Van der Waals forces are weaker still and act between all molecules, polar or not. They become noticeable only when hydrogen bonding is absent, which is why small non-polar molecules are gases at room temperature.

The exam ordering — hydrogen bond strongest, then dipole, then van der Waals weakest — is therefore a ranking of separation distances. Stronger attraction means higher boiling point, and the ranking sorts every comparison question.
bullets: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.
Water boils high because of hydrogen bonding.
Dipole forces are weaker; van der Waals weakest.
Stronger attraction means higher boiling point.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in bonding
paragraphs: The classic trap swaps giving and sharing: candidates call NaCl covalent because 'atoms are joined'. The test is the participants — a metal plus a non-metal always gives, so the bond is ionic. Name the participants first, then the bond.

The second trap is calling any attraction a hydrogen bond. Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to N, O or F; the attraction in HCl is a dipole force, not a hydrogen bond. The bonded atom matters, not the presence of hydrogen alone.

The third trap is the shape swap between NH₃ (pyramidal) and CH₄ (tetrahedral). Counting the atoms is not enough — NH₃ has a lone pair pushing down, which makes it a pyramid with an apex, not a tetrahedron.

The fourth trap is the coordinate bond. It looks like ordinary sharing, but one atom supplies both electrons. In [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ the silver ion accepts pairs from ammonia; the donor is always the ligand, never the metal.
A final trap is calling metal atoms ‘molecules’. Metals are lattices of atoms, not discrete molecules, which is why metals melt as a whole rather than boiling into single atoms.
bullets: Metal + non-metal = ionic, always.
Hydrogen bond needs H on N, O or F.
NH₃ is pyramidal (lone pair); CH₄ is tetrahedral.
In coordinate bonds the ligand donates both electrons.

lessons.title: Separation of Mixtures
lessons.objective: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures, differentiate chemical from physical changes, distinguish pure from impure substances, use melting/boiling points as purity criteria, and specify the principle and everyday use of each separation method (evaporation, distillation, sublimation, re-crystallisation, chromatography, crystallisation, magnetisation, decantation, filtration, centrifugation).

content.heading: Separation of Mixtures
paragraphs: A market woman sells mixed goods — stones in beans, husks in rice — and picks them apart by hand. Separating a chemical mixture is the same job with better tools: every method picks components apart using one difference between them.

content.heading: Elements, compounds and mixtures
paragraphs: An element is a substance made of one kind of atom, like oxygen or iron. A compound is two or more elements joined by chemical bonding, like water or carbon dioxide. A mixture is two or more substances merely mixed, like sand and salt in a bowl.

A chemical change makes a new substance with new properties — burning wood gives ash and smoke. A physical change changes only appearance, like melting ice. Mixtures change physically, so their parts can be separated again.

A pure substance melts and boils at exact temperatures; an impure one melts over a range. A sharp melting point therefore proves purity, while a falling melting point reveals impurities. That is why melting and boiling points are purity tests.
bullets: Element = one kind of atom; compound = bonded elements; mixture = mixed substances.
Chemical change makes new substances; physical change does not.
Pure substances melt sharply; impure ones melt over a range.
content.takeaway: Mixtures separate physically because their parts were never chemically joined.

check.question: Which statement correctly pairs a pure substance with its test?
options: A pure substance melts at one exact temperature
Impure substances boil at one exact temperature
check.why: Purity shows as a sharp melting point; impurities spread the range.

content.heading: Separating by heat and air
paragraphs: Evaporation removes a liquid by heating, leaving the dissolved solid: salt from seawater is won this way. Simple distillation separates liquids with different boiling points, like ethanol and water, by boiling and condensing the vapour. Fractional distillation repeats that for many fractions, as in crude oil refining.

Sublimation turns a solid directly into vapour, as with camphor or ammonium chloride, which then deposits back. Re-crystallisation dissolves the solid hot and cools the solution so pure crystals form. Each method exploits one property: volatility, boiling point or solubility.

Magnetisation removes iron with a magnet, as in scrapyards. Decantation pours the liquid off a solid, filtration traps the solid, and centrifugation spins a mixture so the denser part settles outward, as in blood tests.
bullets: Evaporation leaves the salt; distillation separates by boiling point.
Sublimation: solid → vapour → solid (camphor, NH₄Cl).
Magnet removes iron; decantation pours; filtration traps; centrifugation spins.
Every method exploits one property difference.
content.takeaway: Find the property that differs, and that property is the separating tool.

check.question: To obtain pure water from seawater that also contains suspended sand, which order of methods works?
check.why: Filtration removes sand first, then distillation separates water from dissolved salt.

content.heading: Chromatography and crystallisation
paragraphs: Chromatography separates dyes and inks that travel at different speeds along a strip. Paper chromatography dips ink in water; the colours spread out as bands. Column chromatography does the same through a packed tube that holds back some substances longer.

Simple crystallisation grows crystals from a saturated solution by cooling or evaporation. Re-crystallisation purifies: dissolve the impure solid hot, filter while hot, then cool so only pure crystals form while impurities stay dissolved.
In each case the principle is solubility: components dissolve or travel at different rates. A method is chosen by asking which property differs most between the components.
bullets: Paper chromatography separates ink dyes by travel speed.
Column chromatography holds components back differently.
Crystallisation uses solubility; re-crystallisation purifies.
Choose the method whose property differs most.
content.takeaway: Chromatography separates by speed; crystallisation separates by solubility.

check.question: Black ink is mainly one dye that travels as a single band. What does that tell about its composition?
options: It contains several dyes travelling together
check.why: An ink of several dyes would spread into several bands; a single band suggests one travel rate.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before naming a method, name the property that differs: boiling point, solubility, density or magnetism. The property chooses the method every time.

content.problem: A mixture holds sand, salt and water. Describe a separation that gives pure water.

steps.reason: Sand is insoluble; filter paper traps it while salt water passes
steps.result: Sand is removed as a solid

steps.reason: Water boils and condenses; salt does not distil
steps.result: Pure water is collected, salt remains in the flask

steps.reason: Evaporating to dryness would leave salt mixed with nothing pure to collect
steps.result: Distillation is needed to collect the water itself

content.question: A mixture holds iron filings, sand and water. Give a two-step separation that recovers the iron and the water.
hints: One component answers to a magnet
After that, separate solid from water by filtering
Then distil to collect the water pure

content.heading: Go deeper: Why fractional distillation beats simple
paragraphs: Simple distillation separates two liquids with widely different boiling points. Crude oil holds many fractions with boiling points close together, so one round of boiling cannot divide them. Fractional distillation uses a fractionating column where vapours rise, cool and condense at their own levels.

Each level of the column is a separate still in miniature: vapour condenses, re-boils and rises again. The lightest fraction escapes at the top, while heavier ones leave lower down. The column therefore multiplies the separation without multiplying the apparatus.
The same principle refines air into oxygen and nitrogen, and petroleum into petrol, kerosene and diesel. Whenever boiling points crowd together, fractionation is the answer.
A candidate who links the column to repeated simple distillations will never call a single flask a fractionating column again.

A simple still can split two liquids when their boiling points differ by a wide margin, because the lower-boiling vapour leaves alone. As the gap narrows, contamination rises, and only the column’s repeated boil–condense cycles keep the fractions apart.
bullets: Crude oil fractions boil too close for one still.
The column repeats boil–condense at each level.
Light fractions exit top; heavy fractions exit lower.
Fractionation is repeated simple distillation in one tower.

content.heading: Go deeper: Chromatography as identity evidence
paragraphs: The retention factor, Rf, measures how far a spot travelled relative to the solvent: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent. A spot that always travels to the same Rf is the same substance in different hands, which makes chromatography an identity test, not only a separation tool.

Two dyes with different Rf values separate into different bands, and the pattern of bands is a fingerprint. Food colours, inks and plant pigments are all identified this way in food and forensic laboratories.

Paper chromatography depends on solubility and attraction to paper; column chromatography adds adsorption on the packing. Both exploit the same difference: how strongly each component holds on versus travels on.
The exam trap is to treat Rf as a separation product. Rf identifies; it does not manufacture. Discovery of a new spot means a new dye, not a new element.

Because each substance has a fixed Rf under given conditions, matching Rf values in two samples is strong evidence they contain the same dye. Courts and food laboratories rely on exactly this reasoning.
The solvent must be chosen so spots travel a measurable distance without running off the paper. A solvent in which the dye is insoluble gives no evidence at all.
bullets: Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance.
Rf patterns identify dyes and pigments.
Paper uses solubility; column adds adsorption.
Rf identifies; it does not create new substances.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in separation
paragraphs: The first trap is melting-point reading. A substance melting over a range is impure, but a substance melting sharply is not necessarily pure — some mixtures melt sharply by coincidence. Sharpness is evidence, not proof, and candidates should state it that way.

The second trap confuses sublimation with evaporation. Evaporation turns a liquid into vapour; sublimation turns a solid directly into vapour. Camphor and ammonium chloride sublime; water evaporates. The starting state decides the name.

The third trap mixes decantation with filtration. Decantation pours the liquid off; filtration passes the mixture through a barrier. If the solid is fine enough to pass the filter, decantation fails and centrifugation is the answer.

The fourth trap is choosing distillation for immiscible liquids. Oil and water separate by decantation long before boiling is needed; distillation is the tool when boiling points differ, not whenever two liquids mix.

A final trap is over-heating during evaporation to dryness, which decomposes some salts. Gentle heating and crystallisation on cooling are the safe route, and the question usually hints at it by asking for crystals.
bullets: Sharp melting is evidence, not proof, of purity.
Sublimation starts from a solid; evaporation from a liquid.
Decantation pours; filtration traps; centrifugation spins.
Immiscible liquids separate without boiling.

lessons.title: Solubility
lessons.objective: Distinguish unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated solutions, interpret solubility curves, calculate the amount of solute that dissolves at a given temperature, relate solvents to their uses, and differentiate true solutions from suspensions and colloids with examples.

content.heading: Solubility
paragraphs: A spoon of sugar disappears into tea while grits stay at the bottom. The sugar dissolved; the grits did not. Solubility is simply how much of a substance a given amount of liquid can dissolve — and this lesson explains the limits.

content.heading: Full, not full, and over-full
paragraphs: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve more, like a half-filled cup. A saturated solution is full: at that temperature it can dissolve no more, and any extra solid settles. A supersaturated solution is over-full — it holds more than the limit because it was cooled carefully without anything to start crystallisation.

A solubility curve shows how much dissolves at each temperature. Most salts dissolve more as water warms, so their curve climbs. Gases behave oppositely: oxygen dissolves less in warm water, which is why warm water holds less dissolved air for fish.

Solubility is written in mol/dm³: moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. At saturation, the concentration is fixed by the temperature, not by how much solid you added — extra solid just sits at the bottom.
bullets: Unsaturated: more can dissolve. Saturated: full. Supersaturated: over-full.
Most salts dissolve more when hot; gases dissolve less when hot.
Solubility = moles of solute per dm³ of saturated solution.
content.takeaway: Solubility is a limit set by temperature, and the curve shows how it moves.

check.question: A solution holds more solute than the maximum at that temperature. What is it?
check.why: Holding more than the maximum means the solution is supersaturated.

content.heading: Calculating solubility and choosing solvents
paragraphs: A solubility calculation starts from the definition: how many moles sit in one dm³ of saturated solution. Suppose 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm³. Moles = 11 ÷ 58.5 = 0.188 mol, so the solubility is 0.188 ÷ 0.1 = 1.88 mol/dm³.

Like dissolves like: water, a polar liquid, removes sweat and salt, but not grease. Petrol, an organic solvent, dissolves grease and paint, which is why dry cleaners use it. The solvent is chosen by matching its nature to the stain.

Temperature enters every calculation. A curve reading gives the solubility at the stated temperature, and a supersaturated solution made at a high temperature may crash out crystals as it cools — the basis of re-crystallisation for purification.
bullets: Molar solubility = moles ÷ volume of saturated solution.
Water removes polar stains; petrol removes grease and paint.
The solvent is matched to the nature of the stain.
content.takeaway: Solubility is moles per dm³ at saturation, and the solvent must match the stain.

check.question: Which solvent best removes engine grease from cloth?
check.why: Grease is non-polar like petrol, so petrol dissolves it while water does not.

content.heading: True solutions, suspensions and colloids
paragraphs: A true solution is uniform at the particle level: sugar in water looks clear, passes through filter paper, and never settles. A suspension has particles large enough to see and settle, like muddy water after stirring — Harmattan haze and water paints are suspensions.

A colloid sits between the two: its particles are too small to see or filter but large enough to scatter light. Fog, milk, blood, aerosol sprays, emulsion paints and rubber solution are colloids. The Tyndall effect — a light beam turning visible — is the giveaway.
The particle size decides everything: true solutions pass filter paper; colloids scatter light but do not settle; suspensions settle and are filtered. Size, not appearance, is the distinction.
bullets: True solution: uniform, passes filters, never settles.
Suspension: visible particles, settles, filtered (haze, water paints).
Colloid: invisible particles, scatters light (fog, milk, blood).
Particle size separates the three.
content.takeaway: Size decides: solutions pass, colloids scatter, suspensions settle.

check.question: Which mixture is a colloid?
check.why: Fog scatters light and resists filtration like other colloids, unlike the suspensions and true solution.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Before any solubility number, ask which temperature it belongs to. A solubility quoted without its temperature means nothing, and examiners plant exactly that trap.

content.problem: 11 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.1 dm³ of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.

steps.reason: Moles count particles; Mr(NaCl) = 58.5
Solubility is per cubic decimetre of solution
0.188 × 58.5 = 11.0, so the division is exact

content.question: 23.4 g of NaCl dissolves in 0.2 dm³ of solution. Calculate its molar solubility.
hints: First find moles: 23.4 ÷ 58.5
That is 0.4 mol — check it
Divide by 0.2 dm³

content.heading: Go deeper: Why gases dissolve less when hot
paragraphs: Dissolving a gas means trapping its particles into the liquid. Warming speeds particles up, so they escape more easily — the same reason a hot drink goes flat. Salts behave oppositely because warming helps break their lattice apart.

That opposite behaviour is why solubility curves split into two families: climbing curves for salts, falling curves for gases. Sodium sulfate decahydrate is the exception that proves the rule, falling after about 33 °C when it loses its water of crystallisation.

The practical effect is everywhere: soft drinks are bottled cold to keep gas in, and heating water drives dissolved air out as bubbles. Temperature dependence is not a formula detail; it is visible in every cold drink.
A candidate who explains the escape idea can predict the direction of any curve without memorising it. Hot liquid cannot hold fast-moving gas particles.
The same escape logic explains why heating a soft drink releases bubbles immediately. The gas was only ever loosely held, and warming loosens its grip further.
At the other end, cooling a gas makes it far more soluble, which is why winter lakes hold more dissolved oxygen for fish.
bullets: Gas solubility falls with temperature (particles escape).
Most salts rise; gases fall — two curve families.
Cold drinks stay fizzy because cold holds gas.
One escape picture predicts every direction.

content.heading: Go deeper: Supersaturation and how it forms
paragraphs: A supersaturated solution holds more solute than its temperature allows, but only because crystallisation has not started. Stirring, scratching or adding a tiny crystal starts the process, and the excess falls out until saturation returns.

It is made by dissolving at a high temperature, filtering while hot to remove impurities, then cooling slowly without disturbance. Rock candy is grown exactly this way: a supersaturated sugar solution cooling around a string.
Supersaturation is unstable by definition — the excess wants out. That instability is useful for purification: the excess crashes out as pure crystals while impurities stay dissolved.

The exam trap is calling a supersaturated solution 'concentrated'. Concentration is a measurement; supersaturation is a state beyond the saturation limit. A solution can be concentrated without being supersaturated.
A careful chemist can recrystallise a salt that refuses to dissolve cold: dissolve it hot, remove impurities by hot filtration, then seed the cooling solution with a pure crystal.
Without the seed, a supersaturated solution can sit stable for days — a reminder that stability in chemistry is often only the absence of a beginning.
bullets: Supersaturated = more than the limit, waiting for a start.
Made by hot dissolving, hot filtering, slow cooling.
Used to purify salts by re-crystallisation.
Concentrated is a measure; supersaturated is a state.

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in solubility
paragraphs: The first trap confuses solubility with concentration. Solubility is the saturation limit at a temperature; concentration is what is actually present. A dilute solution may be far below its solubility, and a supersaturated one far above.
The second trap mixes gram solubility with molar solubility. Converting between them needs Mr: grams per dm³ divided by Mr gives mol/dm³. Skipping Mr is the commonest calculation error in this topic.
The third trap ignores the curve's temperature. Reading a value from the wrong temperature point is reading a different solution entirely. Always anchor the reading to the stated temperature.
The fourth trap treats colloids as suspensions. Both look milky, but colloids do not settle and pass neither filter nor light beam silently. Particle size, not appearance, decides the class.
A final trap is treating the Tyndall effect as proof of a true solution. Only colloids scatter a beam of light; a clear true solution leaves the beam invisible.
bullets: Solubility is the limit; concentration is the present amount.
Convert g/dm³ to mol/dm³ by dividing by Mr.
Anchor every curve reading to its temperature.
Colloids scatter light; suspensions settle.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Reduction (Redox)
lessons.objective: Classify reactions in terms of oxidation and reduction in their three senses (oxygen, hydrogen/electron transfer, oxidation number), deduce oxidation numbers, balance simple redox equations, compute electrons transferred, name species and agents, and apply oxidation numbers in naming inorganic compounds.

content.heading: Oxidation and redox
paragraphs: A piece of hot copper is oxidised by oxygen, then restored by hydrogen. JAMB asks whether such a change is oxidation or reduction. This lesson gives three tests, in oxygen, electrons and oxidation numbers, for deciding correctly.

content.heading: From oxygen to electrons
paragraphs: Hot copper foil turns black in air because 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO forms CuO. Copper has gained oxygen, so it has been oxidised. Hydrogen turns CuO back to copper by removing oxygen as CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O, so reduction removes oxygen with hydrogen.

Sodium is oxidised as Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ because it loses an electron, while chlorine is reduced as Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ because it gains that electron. OIL RIG says oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.
bullets: Oxidation as oxygen gain: 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO, while reduction removes oxygen with H2
Oxidation as electron loss: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻, while reduction gains electrons: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain of electrons
content.takeaway: Oxidation gains oxygen or loses electrons; reduction removes oxygen or gains electrons.

check.question: In the reaction 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO, copper is
options: unchanged because oxygen is a spectator
check.why: Copper gains oxygen, and also loses electrons, so it is oxidised.

content.heading: Counting oxidation numbers
paragraphs: A chemist meets potassium manganate(VII), sulphuric acid and dichromate in the same titration set. Oxidation number is a bookkeeping charge assigned by fixed rules: a free element is 0, a monatomic ion equals its charge, hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2, while the sum for a compound is 0. Applying those rules turns each colour change into a charge change that can be compared.
Manganese in KMnO4 obeys 1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7. Sulphur in H2SO4 obeys 2 + S − 8 = 0, so S = +6. Chromium in Cr2O7²⁻ obeys 2Cr − 14 = −2, so Cr = +6.
bullets: Free element is 0, and a monatomic ion takes its charge
Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2 in most compounds
Oxidation numbers sum to 0, or to the ion charge
content.takeaway: Oxidation numbers follow fixed rules, so each atom has a charge to track.

check.question: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H2SO4?
check.why: 2 + S − 8 = 0 gives S = +6.

content.heading: Balancing, naming and agents
paragraphs: Purple potassium manganate(VII) turns pale green with acid and iron(II) salt. Manganese falls from +7 in MnO4⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺ and gains five electrons, while each iron rises from +2 to +3 and loses one electron. Balanced equation: MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O, with five electrons transferred.

Iron at +2 with chloride is iron(II) chloride, while iron at +3 is iron(III) chloride. Potassium manganate(VII) is an oxidising agent: purple MnO4⁻ bleaches to colourless Mn²⁺ when it is reduced. Orange acidified dichromate turns green to Cr³⁺, which also shows an oxidising agent at work.
bullets: Naming follows the ion charge: FeCl2 is iron(II) chloride and FeCl3 is iron(III) chloride
Oxidising agent is reduced while it oxidises another species; reducing agent is oxidised
Tests: purple MnO4⁻ bleaches to colourless Mn²⁺, and orange acidified dichromate turns green to Cr³⁺
content.takeaway: Rise in oxidation number is oxidation; a fall is reduction, and agents prove it.

check.question: In MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O, which species is the oxidising agent?
check.why: MnO4⁻ is reduced from +7 to +2, so it oxidises Fe²⁺.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Look first at oxidation numbers, not at oxygen. If the number rises, call it oxidation even when no oxygen appears; if it falls, call it reduction. Naming iron(II) or iron(III) is then decided by the charge that balances the chloride ions.

content.problem: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in H2S2O3 (thiosulphuric acid)?

steps.reason: Hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is −2, so they are known first.
Oxidation numbers sum to zero in a neutral acid.
Two sulphur atoms share the remaining charge.

content.question: What is the oxidation number of chromium in K2Cr2O7?
hints: Assign potassium +1 and oxygen −2 first
Solve 2Cr = 12 and check the sign

content.heading: Go deeper: Why oxidation number is bookkeeping, not real charge
paragraphs: Manganese in potassium manganate(VII) carries the formal number +7, but no Mn7+ ion exists in the solution. The +7 is obtained by pretending that every bond is fully ionic and giving both shared electrons to the more electronegative partner. In a real manganese-oxygen bond electrons are shared, so manganese keeps some electron density and its physical charge is far smaller than +7.

The rule assigns electrons to the atom whose nucleus attracts them more strongly. Oxygen, being more electronegative than carbon, receives all electrons in each carbon-oxygen bond of carbon dioxide. That assignment gives oxygen −2 and carbon +4, even though the molecule is neutral and no C4+ ion is present. The numbers are correct for electron counting, not for describing isolated ions.

Because the method is a convention, special cases need memorised exceptions. Hydrogen peroxide holds oxygen at −1 rather than −2 because the two oxygen atoms share electrons equally in the oxygen-oxygen bond. Metal hydrides such as sodium hydride place hydrogen at −1 rather than +1 because hydrogen is more electronegative than the metal. Those exceptions do not break the system; they complete it.
bullets: Bookkeeping assigns bonded electrons to the more electronegative atom
Formal charge in covalent molecules need not equal a real ion charge
Peroxide oxygen is −1 and hydride hydrogen is −1, not the usual values

content.heading: Go deeper: Balancing half-equations step by step
paragraphs: Start with the two half-equations written from oxidation numbers. Manganese falls from +7 to +2, so the manganese half-equation must gain electrons: MnO4⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O. Iron rises from +2 to +3, so the iron half-equation must lose electrons: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Both halves already show the correct connectivity.

Electrons gained must equal electrons lost, so the iron half-equation is multiplied by five. Five iron(II) ions give five iron(III) ions and release five electrons: 5Fe²⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + 5e⁻. The five electrons on each side now cancel when the halves are added. Adding the halves gives MnO4⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H2O.

Check the finished equation for atoms and charge before writing it in an answer. Atoms: one manganese, five iron, eight hydrogen and four oxygen appear on each side. Charge: minus one plus ten plus eight equals plus seventeen on the left, and plus two plus fifteen equals plus seventeen on the right. Any mismatch shows that water, hydrogen ions or electrons have been missed.
bullets: Gain of electrons is reduction; loss of electrons is oxidation
Multiply the one-electron iron half-equation by five to match five electrons gained
Balance oxygen with water, hydrogen with H+, then cancel electrons

content.heading: Go deeper: Exam traps in oxidation and agents
paragraphs: The most common trap confuses oxidation with the oxidising agent. Oxidation is the process in which a species rises in oxidation number, while the oxidising agent is the species that causes that rise and is itself reduced. In the iron reaction, iron(II) is oxidised and manganate(VII) is the oxidising agent because manganese falls from +7 to +2. Naming both at once prevents the reversal.

A second trap reverses the oxidation number rule. An increase in oxidation number is oxidation, and a decrease is reduction, whether or not oxygen appears. Hydrogen in copper oxide reduction rises from 0 in H2 to +1 in H2O, so hydrogen is oxidised while copper falls from +2 to 0 and is reduced. Checking the direction first settles the label.

A third trap trusts only the oxygen test and misses electron transfer entirely. Sodium forms sodium chloride with no oxygen present, yet sodium is oxidised as it loses an electron and chlorine is reduced as it gains one. JAMB sets the same pair in different formulae, so the electron and oxidation number tests must be applied beside the oxygen test. That combined habit removes the oxygen-only error.
bullets: Oxidation is the rise; the oxidising agent is reduced
Decrease in oxidation number is reduction, even without oxygen
Reducing agent is oxidised while it reduces another species

lessons.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
lessons.objective: Distinguish the properties of acids and bases, determine basicity, classify normal, acidic, basic and double salts, state methods of preparing salts, relate conductance to degree of dissociation, perform pH and pOH calculations, state the significance of pH, apply buffer solutions, choose indicators, and balance the hydrolysis of salts.

content.heading: Acids, Bases and Salts
paragraphs: A housewife in Onitsha adds vinegar to remove a stain but avoids touching a caustic soda spill on her hands. One is an acid, the other a base. What separates them is how each behaves in water.

content.heading: What acids and bases do
paragraphs: An acid is a substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H₃O⁺ ions, or a proton donor. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid, for example an oxide or a hydroxide. Acids turn blue litmus red and form salts with metals and carbonates.

Bases feel soapy, turn red litmus blue and form salts with acids. The number of replaceable hydrogen atoms an acid has is its basicity, so HCl is monobasic while H₂SO₄ is dibasic. Acids and bases therefore cancel each other in neutralisation.

Indicators tell the difference without tasting anything. Litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are the standard trio, and a buffer solution is a mixture that resists pH change when acid or alkali is added. Vinegar contains ethanoic acid, while citrus fruits contain citric acid.
bullets: An acid furnishes H₃O⁺; a base neutralises an acid
Basicity counts the replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule
Litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein are standard indicators
A buffer solution resists change in pH
content.takeaway: Acids donate protons, bases accept them, and indicators show which is which.

check.question: Which definition of an acid follows the proton-donor idea?
options: A substance whose aqueous solution furnishes H₃O⁺ ions
A substance that turns red litmus blue
A substance that neutralises an acid
A substance that conducts electricity only when molten
check.why: Furnishing H₃O⁺ is exactly donating a proton to water.

content.heading: Salts and how they are made
paragraphs: A salt is the neutral product of reacting an acid with a base, metal or carbonate. When all replaceable hydrogen is used, the salt is normal, like NaCl. When some remains, it is acidic, like NH₄Cl, while basic salts still carry OH.

A double salt holds two salts together, and alums are the example. Salts are prepared by neutralisation, by precipitation, or by dissolving a metal or carbonate in an acid. Zn + dilute H₂SO₄ gives ZnSO₄ and hydrogen.

Whether a solution conducts depends on how far it dissociates. A strong acid like HCl dissociates fully and conducts well, while a weak acid like ethanoic acid dissociates partly and conducts weakly. Concentration is about how much is present, not how strongly it dissociates.
bullets: Normal salts use all replaceable hydrogen; acidic salts keep some
Alums are double salts crystallised together
Salts are prepared by neutralisation, precipitation or acid on metal
Conductance follows the amount of ions, not just concentration
content.takeaway: Salt type names its leftover hydrogen or hydroxide, and strength means dissociation.

check.question: NH₄Cl is an example of which salt type?
check.why: Ammonium chloride carries replaceable hydrogen, so it is an acidic salt.

content.heading: pH, titration and hydrolysis
paragraphs: The pH scale measures hydrogen-ion concentration as pH = −log[H⁺]. A solution with [H⁺] = 1×10⁻³ mol/dm³ has pH 3, and pOH = 14 − pH. Neutral water is 7.

pH matters daily: the stomach works near pH 1–2, soil suits crops near 6–7, and blood holds 7.4. In titration an indicator marks the end point, so phenolphthalein suits a strong acid with a strong base. The mole ratio at the end point gives the unknown concentration.

Hydrolysis is the reaction of a salt with water, and it decides the character. NH₄Cl hydrolyses acidic, while Na₂CO₃ hydrolyses basic. Their equations are NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ and CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻.
bullets: pH = −log[H⁺] and pOH = 14 − pH at 298 K
Blood holds pH 7.4; the stomach works near pH 1–2
Titration uses the mole ratio at the indicator end point
NH₄Cl gives an acidic solution; Na₂CO₃ gives a basic one
content.takeaway: pH counts hydrogen ions, titration counts moles, and hydrolysis sets the character.

check.question: A solution has [H⁺] = 1×10⁻³ mol/dm³. What is its pH?

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In a titration, write the mole ratio first, then the volumes. The ratio decides everything, so a 1:1 reaction is a straight volume swap while a 2:1 reaction halves one side.

content.problem: 20.0 cm³ of 0.10 M hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide. Find the concentration of the NaOH.

steps.reason: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is a 1:1 ratio
moles = concentration × volume in dm³ (20.0 cm³ = 0.020 dm³)
0.0020 mol sits in 25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³, so C = n/V

content.question: 25.0 cm³ of 0.20 M sulphuric acid is neutralised by an unknown base in a 1:2 ratio (H₂SO₄ : base = 1:2). It takes 40.0 cm³ of the base. Find its concentration.
hints: First find the moles of acid: 0.25 × 0.025
The base has twice as many moles as the acid
Then divide those moles by 0.040 dm³

content.heading: Go deeper: Why conductance follows dissociation
paragraphs: Conductance needs ions to carry charge to the electrodes. A strong acid like HCl dissociates almost completely, so many ions move and conductance is high. A weak acid like ethanoic acid dissociates only partly, so few ions move and conductance is low even at the same concentration.

That is why degree of dissociation and acid strength move together. A measured rise in conductance on dilution is not a rise in strength; it is the same weak acid spreading out, so a larger fraction dissociates. Conductance therefore tracks ions present, not the label strong or weak.

The dilution effect explains a common curve: molar conductance rises slowly as the solution gets more dilute. A candidate who links the two ideas will not call ethanoic acid strong just because its conductance climbs on dilution.

Strong and weak bases behave the same way. NH₄OH is weak and conducts poorly although it is a base, while NaOH is strong and conducts well. Strength is about dissociation, and concentration is only about amount.
bullets: Conductance counts the ions actually present
Strong acids dissociate fully; weak acids partly
Dilution raises the dissociated fraction of a weak acid
Strength and concentration are different ideas

content.heading: Go deeper: Choosing the indicator for a titration
paragraphs: An indicator changes colour across a pH range, so it must change close to the end point of the reaction. Methyl orange changes between pH 3.1 and 4.4, phenolphthalein between 8.2 and 10.0, and litmus changes broadly near 7.

A strong acid with a strong base ends near pH 7, so either indicator works. A weak acid with a strong base ends above pH 7, so phenolphthalein is correct and methyl orange would change too early. A strong acid with a weak base ends below pH 7, so methyl orange is correct.

The titraton curve makes the choice visible: it jumps through the end-point range sharply for strong–strong pairs and more gently for weak pairs. A candidate who reads the jump sees why the wrong indicator gives a false end point.

Litmus is a mixture and changes gradually, so it is a poor titration indicator. Methyl orange and phenolphthalein stay the sharp choices in the examination hall, and the curve tells which one to pick.
bullets: Methyl orange changes near pH 3–4; phenolphthalein near pH 8–10
Weak acid + strong base needs phenolphthalein
Strong acid + weak base needs methyl orange
The titration curve shows where the jump falls

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap between basic salt and base
paragraphs: A basic salt is not a base. Na₂CO₃ is a basic salt because its solution is alkaline after hydrolysis, but it does not contain free OH⁻ ions in the way NaOH does. Calling it a base confuses the name of the salt with the behaviour of its solution.

The same confusion strikes acidic salts. NH₄Cl is not an acid, even though its solution is acidic. Acidity here comes from the NH₄⁺ ion releasing a proton to water, not from the salt itself being an acid.

The exam loves that pair: solution character asked, salt type implied. The safe habit is to name the ion that hydrolyses and write its equation before deciding. CO₃²⁻ takes a proton from water and leaves OH⁻, so the solution turns basic.

That equation is also the answer to the balancing item. Hydrolysis equations balance atoms and charge together, so a candidate who writes the ion first rarely writes an unbalanced equation in the hall.
bullets: A basic salt is not a base in solution
An acidic salt is not an acid
Hydrolysis of the ion decides the solution character
Write the ion equation before choosing the answer

lessons.title: Electrolysis
lessons.objective: Distinguish electrolytes from non-electrolytes, perform Faraday calculations with Q = It, identify suitable electrodes, predict the products at the electrodes for dilute H₂SO₄, aqueous CuSO₄, CuCl₂, dilute and concentrated NaCl, and fused NaCl, state the factors that affect discharge of ions, describe purification of copper and production of aluminium, sodium, oxygen, chlorine and NaOH, use the electrochemical series and electrode potentials for simple calculations, and identify methods of protecting metals from corrosion.

content.heading: Electrolysis
paragraphs: A technician in a Lagos plating workshop dips a dull key into a chromium bath and comes out with a shining one. Electricity has moved metal ions onto the key. That process is electrolysis.

content.heading: Electrolytes and the cell
paragraphs: An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity when molten or in aqueous solution and is decomposed in the process. A non-electrolyte, like sugar or ethanol, does not conduct even when dissolved. The anode is the positive electrode and the cathode is the negative electrode.

Electrolysis is the decomposition of an electrolyte by an electric current. Inert electrodes, such as platinum or carbon, do not react and only pass the current. Reactive electrodes, such as copper, dissolve at the anode instead of discharging an anion.

Which ion is discharged follows the electrochemical series and concentration. At the cathode, metal ions and hydrogen compete, and the lower one in the series is discharged. At the anode, non-metal anions are discharged, but concentrated solutions favour the anion over water.
bullets: An electrolyte conducts only when molten or dissolved
The anode is positive; the cathode is negative
Inert electrodes do not react; reactive electrodes do
Discharge follows the electrochemical series and concentration
content.takeaway: The electrolyte, the electrodes and the voltage decide what comes off at each pole.

check.question: When copper electrodes are used to electrolyse copper(II) chloride solution, what happens at the anode?
check.why: A reactive copper anode dissolves instead of letting chloride ions discharge.

content.heading: Products for the standard electrolytes
paragraphs: Dilute H₂SO₄ gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, so water is the electrolyte that reacts. Aqueous CuSO₄ gives copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. CuCl₂ solution gives copper and chlorine.

Dilute NaCl solution gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, while concentrated brine gives hydrogen and chlorine. Fused NaCl gives sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode because there is no water to compete. Electrode statements are written as half-equations.
Faraday laws link charge to amount: Q = It, where I is in amperes and t in seconds. One Faraday (96500 C) discharges one mole of electrons, so gas volumes follow from the moles formed.
bullets: Dilute H₂SO₄ gives H₂ at cathode and O₂ at anode
Conc. brine gives H₂ and Cl₂; fused NaCl gives Na and Cl₂
Q = It, and 1 F = 96500 C discharges 1 mol of electrons
Electrode statements are written as half-equations
content.takeaway: Name the electrolyte and the electrode, then read the products off the series.

check.question: Electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution gives which pair of products?
options: Sodium at cathode, chlorine at anode
Hydrogen at cathode, chlorine at anode
Hydrogen at cathode, oxygen at anode
Sodium at cathode, oxygen at anode
check.why: Water is reduced to hydrogen, and concentrated chloride discharges chlorine.

content.heading: Uses, series and protecting iron
paragraphs: Electrolysis purifies copper: impure copper dissolves at the anode while pure copper deposits at the cathode. Aluminium is extracted from aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite, and sodium by the Downs process on fused NaCl. Chlorine and NaOH come from brine.
The electrochemical series, K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb, H, Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, predicts reactivity and displacement. A metal higher up displaces a lower one, so zinc displaces iron but not sodium.

Corrosion is electrochemical: iron rusts where oxygen and water meet the metal. Painting, greasing or oiling blocks air and water, while cathodic protection sacrifices a more reactive metal like zinc. Electroplating coats a base metal with a rust-resistant one.
bullets: Purification of copper uses impure anode and pure cathode
Aluminium comes from oxide in cryolite; sodium from fused NaCl
A higher metal displaces a lower one from solution
Iron is protected by paint, grease or a sacrificial metal
content.takeaway: Electrolysis purifies, extracts and protects, all by choosing the right metal and electrolyte.

check.question: Which method protects iron from rusting by being sacrificed in its place?
options: Coating with a thin grease layer
check.why: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes first and spares the iron.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: For any Faraday item, convert the time to seconds first. A current for five minutes is 300 seconds, and mixing minutes with seconds is the commonest silent error.

content.problem: A current of 2.0 A is passed through dilute H₂SO₄ for 965 s. Calculate the volume of hydrogen discharged at the cathode at s.t.p.

steps.reason: Q = It, with the time in seconds

steps.operation: Convert charge to moles of electrons
steps.reason: 1 F = 96500 C discharges 1 mol of electrons
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂, so 0.020 mol e⁻ gives 0.010 mol H₂, and 1 mol = 22.4 dm³ at s.t.p.

content.question: A current of 1.5 A flows for 1930 s through aqueous CuSO₄. Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; Ar Cu = 63.5)
hints: First find Q = It in coulombs
Divide by 96500 to get moles of electrons
Halve it for moles of Cu, then multiply by 63.5

content.heading: Go deeper: Why concentrated brine gives chlorine
paragraphs: In dilute NaCl solution the anode discharges oxygen from water because water is present in large amount and oxidises more easily. In concentrated brine the chloride ions crowd the anode, and their concentration lets them win. Discharge is therefore a contest between ions, and concentration tips the balance.

The same contest explains the cathode in fused NaCl. Water is absent, so sodium ions discharge directly. That is the whole logic of the Downs process: melt the salt, remove the water, and the metal itself must discharge.

Oxygen overpotential also matters. Discharging oxygen from water needs extra voltage, so in concentrated brine the chloride route needs less. A candidate who thinks in terms of contests rather than lists will predict products for unfamiliar electrolytes.

The Hofmann voltameter shows the contest plainly: hydrogen and oxygen collect in a 2:1 ratio from water. The ratio is the stoichiometry made visible, and it confirms the half-equations without any memorisation.
bullets: Concentrated chloride outcompetes water at the anode
Fused NaCl leaves sodium no rival at the cathode
Water oxidation needs extra voltage (overpotential)
Hofmann voltameter gives H₂:O₂ in a 2:1 ratio

content.heading: Go deeper: Purification of copper step by step
paragraphs: Impure copper is cast into thick slabs and hung as the anode in copper(II) sulfate solution. Pure copper is rolled into thin sheets for the cathode. On passing current, copper atoms dissolve from the anode and an equal mass deposits on the cathode.

Copper ions move through the solution, so the number of Cu²⁺ ions stays constant. Impurities that are less reactive than copper, like gold and silver, fall off the anode as anode sludge. Impurities more reactive than copper, like zinc, dissolve but do not deposit at the cathode.

The product is 99.99% pure copper, which is why the process is called electrorefining. Resistivity falls sharply with purity, so the copper is good for wires and electrical work where ordinary copper would waste energy as heat.

The same cell proves the series in action. Only copper among the dissolved metals can discharge at the cathode under these conditions, which is why the deposit is pure. Reactivity, not just voltage, decides the outcome.
bullets: Impure copper is the anode; pure copper is the cathode
Copper dissolves and redeposits, keeping Cu²⁺ constant
Less reactive impurities fall as sludge; more reactive ones dissolve
Electrorefining gives 99.99% pure copper

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap between cell and electrolysis poles
paragraphs: In a galvanic cell the anode is negative and oxidation happens there, while in electrolysis the anode is positive and oxidation still happens there. The electrode label follows the reaction, not the sign: the anode is where oxidation occurs in both devices. Mixing the two rules is the commonest pole error.

The other trap is writing the cell sign on the electrodes of a powered cell. A power supply fixes the cathode as negative and the anode as positive, but the names cathode and anode still mean reduction and oxidation respectively. Signs follow the supply, names follow the reaction.

Corrosion arguments use the same map. In a rusting nail the iron is the anode because it oxidises. Cathodic protection works by attaching a piece whose anode reaction is preferred, so the protective metal is eaten while the iron is spared.

A candidate who repeats oxidation happens at the anode in both cases will answer pole questions without memorising two contradictory lists. One rule covers both devices, and that is why it is worth learning.
bullets: The anode is where oxidation happens in any cell
Signs differ: negative in a cell, positive in electrolysis
Corrosion makes iron the anode; protection changes the anode
Oxidation at the anode is the one rule to keep
